Anthropogenic	 stressors can magnify the effects of such top- down pressure on foundation species. The gastropod Coralliophila violacea (Kiener, 1836) depletes coral energy reserves via predation, potentially increasing coral susceptibility to land- based pollution (i.e., sediment accumulation and nutrient pollution). We hypothesized that sedimentation would worsen coral mortality, while nutrient enrichment would mitigate the harmful effects of sediment and predation on coral mortality by increasing the densities of algal symbionts. To test these hypotheses, we conducted in situ surveys of the fring-ing reefs in Mo'orea, French Polynesia to explore the relationships among massive Porites spp. cover, C. violacea densities, and sediment accumulation on coral colonies across low and high nutrient sites. We also conducted a factorial field experiment to test the interactions among these stressors on coral tissue mortality, symbiont densi-ties, and chlorophyll. Massive Porites colonies at higher nutrient sites had C. violacea densities 13 times higher than at low nutrient sites but there was no difference in the amount of live tissue on coral colonies with or without snails among these sites. In our experiment, there were interactions between predation and nutrients as well as nutrients and sediment that impacted coral mortality. Sedimentation and preda-tion by C. violacea increased coral tissue mortality independently by ~20%. Nutrient enrichment reduced this effect in corals under sedimentation or predation pressure by lowering coral tissue mortality by 18% and increasing algal symbiont densities by ~28%. Our results indicate that sediment does not magnify top- down pressure on this coral, and that moderate nutrient enrichment may interact with predation in complex, unexpected ways to alter the responses of corals to top- down pressure.

2.2 | Field surveys of snails, nutrient availability, and sedimentation across reefs To assess the spatial relationships among corallivorous snails, nu-trient enrichment, and sedimentation at the reef scale, we con-ducted in situ surveys across seven fringing reefs at ~1– 2 m depth on the north shore of Mo'orea (Figure 1a). In preliminary surveys, Coralliophila violacea was only observed on massive Porites colonies >10 cm in diameter. Thus, we surveyed all massive Porites colonies >10 cm in diameter found in 25 × 2 m belt transects parallel to shore (n = 4 transects per site). For each colony, we recorded the flat col-ony diameter parallel to the benthos to the nearest cm, estimated percent live tissue of the coral colony, and counted the number of C. violacea snails found on each colony. Colony diameter was used to estimate the colony surface area using the surface area of a hemi-sphere (2πr2), which we found closely resembled the shape of all the massive Porites colonies in our study. This area was then multiplied by the estimated value for percent live tissue to estimate the surface area of live tissue.

Benthic photograph quadrats (25 × 25 cm) were taken on al-ternating sides at one- meter intervals on each transect using an Olympus TG- 4 camera to quantify massive Porites cover at the sites. These photograph quadrats were processed in the CoralNet Software using the stratified random point distribution setting with 50 points per frame and a confidence threshold of 95% for computer automation (n = 1,402 photographs total) (Beijbom et al., 2015). These same photograph quadrats were used to de-termine sediment prevalence on massive Porites colonies using the “Fiji” version of ImageJ software (Schindelin et al., 2012). To keep the colony size class consistent with those used from our in situ surveys, each massive Porites colony >10 cm diameter was evaluated for presence or absence of sediment on the colony (i.e., sediment accumulation) (Figure 1b). For each occurrence of sedi-ment accumulation on massive Porites, we noted if the coral tissue adjacent to the sediment was pale as this is often an indicator of physiological stress.

We focused our study on the common reef- building coral mas-sive Porites because it is a dominant coral in the Mo'orea fringing reefs yet has been in decline in these habitats over the past decade (Edmunds, 2020). In Mo'orea, the lagoon is dominated by several species of massive Porites with Porites lutea (Edwards, 1,860) and Porites lobata (Dana, 1846) being the most common (Bosserelle et al., 2014). Distinguishing among these species by corallite morphology is challenging in situ, and corallite morphology of Porites spp. does not always conform to distinct genetic clades (Forsman et al., 2009).

Thus, we focused on massive Porites colonies that shared common color and morphology. Massive Porites are frequently preyed upon by Coralliophila violacea (Kiener, 1836) (McClanahan, 1994), which is chemically attracted to massive Porites (Hamman, 2018). This cor-allivorous gastropod feeds on a single coral colony for extended periods of time, impairing the physiological performance of the col-ony and increasing tissue loss and mortality (Clements & Hay, 2018; Hamman, 2018, 2019; Oren et al., 1998; Raymundo et al., 2016).

Nutrient treatments were established at the cinderblock scale with every other cinderblock in the row assigned to the enriched treatment. For enriched blocks, we affixed two nutrient diffus-ers to opposite sides of each cinderblock. Nutrient diffusers were 10 cm long ×2.5 cm wide PVC pipe with 10 0.6 cm holes drilled into the sides. While the proximal environmental triggers of bleaching are reasonably well understood, considerably less is known concerning physiological and ecological factors that might exacerbate coral bleaching or delay recovery. Results Temperature patterns Coral bleaching was evident in that colonies appeared visibly pale in October compared to August, and re-gained considerable color by January (Fig. 1). The observed coral bleaching coincided with high seawater temperatures at 18 m depth, which were unusually high during August–November 2004 compared to the same periods in 2000–2003 (Fig. 2). Most coral bleaching models agree that bleaching occurs when corals are exposed to water temperatures 1–2"C above the average local maximum for extended periods (Hoegh-Guldberg 1999). The HotSpot temperature threshold for this Belizean reef, reflecting the average local maximum temperature at 2 m depth, has previously been estimated to be 29.85"C (Aronson et al. 2002). Our data show that in 2004, daily average water temperature measured at 18 m exceeded this threshold for a total of 36 days, including a period of 19 consecutive days in 2004 (Sep-tember 15–October 3). This is likely an underestimate of the number of potentially stressful days, as the 29.85"C threshold is based on 2 m depth, and the average local maximum temperature at 18 m is lower than this threshold. Reductions in zooxanthellae density are often asso-ciated with bleaching, though it has been shown that zooxanthellae densities fluctuate seasonally (Fagoonee et al. 1999; Fitt et al. 2000). Studies have documented regular reductions of symbiont density during the warmest times of year, a phenomenon assumed to be pantropical in corals (Fagoonee et al. 1999; Fitt et al. 2000). Although the bleaching extent did not reach catastrophic levels, the zooxanthellae reductions and visible bleaching that we observed likely go beyond seasonal lows, intensified by the abnormally high sea-water temperatures and possibly by Hurricane Ivan storm surge as well. It is important to note that overall, the zooxanthellae densities that we observed before, during, and after bleaching are higher than reported elsewhere in the Caribbean for this genus (Fitt et al. 1993, 2000). Nonetheless, the pale appearance of our colonies in October (Fig. 1) along with the observed reduction in zooxanthellae density (Fig. 3) suggests that corals experienced considerable bleaching stress.

Montastraea faveolata and Montastraea franksi are the major reef building corals in this habitat, and 21 out of 63 (!33%) colonies examined exhibited recent grazing scars. In the Caribbean, herbivorous fishes (parrotfishes and surgeonfishes) are critical to maintaining healthy coral reefs, as they benefit corals by removing competi-tively superior macroalgae (Lewis 1986; Hughes 1994). However, some parrotfish also consume live coral, with direct detrimental effects on coral growth and survival (Meesters et al. 1994; McClanahan et al. 2005; Rotjan and Lewis 2005). Parrotfish preferentially graze certain coral species (Garzon-Ferreira and Reyes-Nivia 2001; Rotjan and Lewis 2006), as well as particular colonies within a species (Sanchez et al. 2004; Rotjan and Lewis 2005). Parrotfish predation produces characteristic, highly conspicuous grazing scars (Fig. 1a), and often results in partial colony mortality. Although the proxi-mal cause of feeding selectivity is not known, parrotfish often repeatedly graze the same coral colonies (Bruckner and Bruckner 1998; Bruckner et al. 2000; Sanchez et al. 2004; Rotjan and Lewis 2005). Because corals are clonal organisms, partial predation by parrotfish is likely to be an important source of chronic stress for reef corals.

In this study, we document a non-catastrophic coral bleaching event in Belize in September 2004 that coin-cided with elevated seawater temperatures, storm surge from Hurricane Ivan, and seasonal variability in zoo-xanthellae densities. In the context of these stressors, we examined the effects of chronic parrotfish grazing on the coral-algal symbiosis. Specifically, we tested whether Montastraea spp. coral colonies exposed to chronic parrotfish grazing showed a greater reduction in sym-biont density during this bleaching event compared to intact conspecific colonies over time. Finally, we inves-tigated the genetic stability of Symbiodinium spp. com-munities in grazed versus intact coral colonies over the course of this bleaching event.

By inflicting damage to prey tissues, consumer species may increase stress in prey hosts and reduce overall fitness (i.e., primary effects, such as growth or reproduction) or cause secondary effects by affecting prey interactions with other species such as microbes. However, little is known about how abiotic conditions affect the outcomes of these biotic interactions. In coral reef communities, both nutrient enrichment and predation have been linked to reduced fitness and disease facilitation in corals, yet no study to date has tested their combined effects on corals or their associated microbial communities (i.e., microbiomes). Here, we assess the effects of grazing by a prevalent coral predator (the short coral snail, Coralliophila abbreviata) and nutrient enrichment on staghorn coral, Acropora cervicornis, and its microbiomes using a factorial experiment and high- throughput DNA sequencing. We found that predation, but not nutrients, significantly reduced coral growth and increased mortality, tissue loss, and turf algae colonization. Partial predation and nutrient enrichment both independently altered coral  microbiomes such that one bacterial genus came to dominate the microbial community. Nutrient- enriched corals were associated with significant increases in Rickettsia-like organ-isms, which are currently one of several microbial groups being investigated as a disease agent in this coral species. However, we found no effects of nutrient enrichment on coral health, disease, or their predators. This research suggests that in the several months following coral transplantation (i.e., restoration) or disturbance (i.e., recovery), Caribbean acroporid corals appear to be highly susceptible to negative effects caused by predators, but not or not yet sus-ceptible to nutrient enrichment despite changes to their microbial communities.

Statistical analysis Coral fragments that went missing due to roaming turtles and storms were removed from statistical analyses (snail + nutrient: n = 3; snail- only: n = 2; nutrient- only: n = 0; control: n = 3). Colony mortality was defined as a total loss of living tissue from the coral fragment and was analyzed using a generalized linear model (GLM) with a binomial distribution due to uneven sample sizes between treatments. Tissue loss was only observed on snail addition colonies during our experiment; therefore, we examined the effects of nutrients on tissue predation. To do this, we estimated the area of tissue predation using the equation for the area of an ellipse (A = πab) to approximate the natural shape of C. abbreviata feeding scars. We used measurements of the maximum height and width of scars taken at the end of the experiment or before tissue sloughing was observed on corals. When predation scars extended across the circumference of the coral, we averaged the maximum and minimum scar height and multiplied it by the circumference measured at the base of each individual coral. Tissue loss data were square root transformed to meet the assumptions of par-ametric statistics and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was used to analyze the effect of nutrient enrichment and coral genotype on tissue predation. To examine treatment effects on coral growth, corals that suffered full colony mortality or were broken and reattached in the middle of the experiment were excluded from this analysis. Growth data were analyzed using a GLM (nutrients × pre-dation + genotype). The percent cover of filamentous turf algae on coral colonies was analyzed using beta regression with the betareg package in R (Cribari- Neto and Zeileis 2010), as beta regression is used to model continuous sample proportions. All analyses were conducted in R version 3.2.1 (R Core Team 2015).

Coral microbiome collections and processing To determine the effects of nutrients and predators on coral microbiomes, we randomly selected five colonies from each treatment (including both genotypes) for sam-pling at the end of the experiment. Part of the main branches of corals were clipped and placed in 50 mL cen-trifuge tubes and frozen until analysis. Feeding scars were included in samples for all snail addition treatments. We did not sample corals with disease signs as rapid mor-tality occurred before sampling could be conducted. We used high- throughput 16S amplicon sequencing to assess the bacterial and archaeal communities associated with each coral. To do this, we isolated and homogenized coral tissue from both the tip and the base of each coral fragment with a WaterPik and sterile Milli- Q water. Total DNA was extracted from 200 μL of the resulting tissue slurry with a MoBio PowerSoil kit according to manufacturer’s protocol. Barcoded primers 515F and 806R and ToughMix PCR (Quanta BioSciences, Gaithersburg, Maryland, USA) were used to amplify and tag the V4 region of the bacterial and archaeal 16S rRNA gene. Samples were amplified in triplicate, with each tech-nical replicate given a different combination of barcodes. Triplicates were pooled, cleaned, and quantified before all samples were combined in equimolar ratios. Multiplexed libraries were submitted to Oregon State University’s Center for Genome Research and Biocomputing (CGRB) for sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq platform.

To assess treatment effects on coral microbiomes, we performed Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) using QIIME’s beta_diversity_through_plots.py. We calcu-lated weighted UniFrac distances and principal coordi-nates after rarefying the raw OTU table to a uniform depth of 43,000 reads per sample. Data were loaded into R using the Phyloseq package v1.12.2 (McMurdie and Holmes 2014, R Core Team 2015). We used Levene’s tests and ANOVAs to assess treatment affects for PCoA axes using the car package v2.0.25 in R. Correlations between OTUs and PCoA axes were determined with QIIME using the rarefied table and observation_metadata_corre-lation.py. Correlations with family- level taxa were assessed by pooling these OTUs with summarize_taxa.py.

Prior to differential abundance analysis, OTUs present in fewer than four samples (>0.5n) were removed from the pre- rarefaction OTU table. Additionally, we used only OTUs that were found in at least 25% of samples and with counts of at least 10 (out of 30,000 reads). R packages Phyloseq and DESeq2 v1.8.2 (Love et al. 2014) were used to perform Wald tests for differential abundance of indi-vidual OTUs using the model formula ~nutrients + snails + nutrients:snails. The effect of genotype on microbial communities was not explored due to limited sample sizes. Correlation of OTUs with coral growth rate, tissue loss, and algal colonization was assessed in QIIME by rare-fying the filtered OTU table to 30,000 reads per sample and using observation_metadata_correlation.py. All reported P- values are FDR- corrected.

Predation × nutrient experiment To assess how predation and nutrients affect corals and their microbiomes, we exposed colonies of A. cervicornis to a fully factorial field experiment from June to August 2013. Due to the threatened status of this species, this exper-iment could not be conducted in natural reef settings or with already- restored colonies. Thus, we  conducted this experiment in the Coral Restoration Foundation’s coral nursery in Key Largo, FL, USA in an open sand flat (30- ft depth) using corals grown through established propa-gation techniques (Johnson et al. 2011). We collected coral fragments using wire cutters from  visually healthy (e.g., non- diseased) colonies of two  genotypes (Upper Keys 2, “U- 2”; Upper Keys 8, “U- 8”) due to possible genotypic variation in disease susceptibility. All coral fragments were ~10 cm long to approximate coral transplant sizes used in restoration activities and due to limits in using nursery corals. Using All Fix Marine Epoxy, we secured each coral fragment to an individual structure consisting of a con-crete slab with attached vertical PVC pipes, with corals attached to the top of one PVC pipe. Structures were placed 3 m apart in all directions and were cleaned of all fouling organisms prior to experimentation.

METHODS Survey of corallivory on staghorn colonies To determine the prevalence of predation on Acropora cervicornis by Coralliophila abbreviata in natural settings, we conducted surveys of both natural and restored colonies across four coral reefs in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary (Molasses Reef: N 25 0.579, W 80 22.471; Pickles Reef: N 24 59.170, W 80 24.940; Conch Reef: N 24 57.110, W 80 27.564; American Shoals: N 24 31.568, W 81 31.383). At each site, we sur-veyed all A. cervicornis colonies found in 15–20, 2 × 20 m belt transects and recorded the density of C. abbreviata per colony, as well as colony height, length, and width to the nearest cm.

We found that partial, sub- lethal predation on healthy corals could lead to rapid colony mortality when grazing wounds became large (here, ~30% of coral surface area). In our experiment, corals with partial tissue predation by Coralliophila abbreviata were nearly five times more likely to suffer complete mortality than corals without pred-ators. While the densities of corallivorous snails used in our experimental predator additions were on the high end of naturally observed densities found in our survey (exper-iment: 0.2 snails/cm of coral; survey: 0.14 ± 0.08 snails/cm of coral), our results are similar to other studies showing particularly high feeding rates on acroporid corals by C. abbreviata (Brawley and Adey 1982, Knowlton et al.

RESULTS Surveys of predation on staghorn corals A total of 198 Acropora cervicornis colonies were recorded across the four reefs surveyed. Of these, 15.2% (n = 30) were found harboring Coralliophila abbreviata. Growth patterns vary a great deal within species according to a host of environmental factors. Daily growth ridges in the epithecae (Barnes, 1972) and high and low density growth bands develop according to the favourability of conditions. Thus, the linear extension of the skeleton can be used as a measure of growth for the coral head. At times there is not a simple relationship between size and age for corals as partial mortality, colony fission and colony fusion may distort measures of growth (Hughes & Jackson, 1980). In this study, care was taken to not sample damaged branches.

This study aimed to investigate allocation of energy in corals at Rottnest Island. Corals can use energy for three main functions: in growth, reproduction and storage of lipid (Sibly & Calow, 1986). Allocation of input to these three functions was mea- sured simultaneously in a population of corals over a period of 13 months. Growth was measured as linear extension, storage of lipid was estimated gravimetrically as the percentage of tissue made up of lipid and reproductive activity was investigated by measuring ova production, production of planulae and the lipid content of those planu- lae. Stages of gametogenesis were also monitored.

Larval capture To estimate the number of larvae produced, portions of colonies were taken from each coral 4 days before the new moon in March and transported to the laboratory. Colonies were placed in fresh sea water and larvae were collected, counted and stored in a solution of 10% formaldehyde in sea water.

On each slide all polyps (50-100) were scored for their stage of gametogenesis and their planulae were counted. Stages were identified basically following those of Stoddart (1984a,b). There were four stages of spermatogenesis and two stages of oogenesis. Reproduction includes both production of planulae and gametes, so a measure of reproductive output which included both components was devised. An index of repro- ductive potential (IRP) was calculated from the percentage of polyps with ova and planulae for each colony at each date. The largest sum of the percentage of polyps containing the two oogenic stages and/or planulae at each time point of each coral was termed the IRP.

The index of reproductive potential (IRP) was significantly larger in fragmented than unfragmented corals. In dislodged corals the IRP was smaller than that of the corals which were not dislodged but not significantly so. There was no significant effect of site (Table 4). These trends are the same as those found for the data on capture of larvae shed in the laboratory (Fig. 4). Corals with the four damage treatments: fragmentation only, dislodgement only, dislodgement and fragmentation and no damage followed similar gametogenesis pat- terns. All groups showed the disappearance of late sperm and ova on 7th February and 5th April and all had major planulation in March (Ward, 1992). All four groups planulated in February as well as March although the February event was consider- ably smaller.

Abstract. Indirect biotic interactions play a crucial role in structuring ecological communities, but many of these interactions have not been explored. Algal competition and corallivory are two major stressors contributing to the decline of coral reefs. Here, we provide the first evidence of algal-induced corallivory and synergistic effects between the two stressors on corals. When corals (Montastraea faveolata) were placed in contact with algae (Halimeda opuntia) together with corallivorous fireworms (Hermodice carunculata) in aquaria, corals suffered high tissue mortality. This mortality was reduced in the presence of algae only, and no mortality occurred in the presence of fireworms only or when excluding both algae and fireworms. These findings were supported by field observations showing a predominance of fireworms inside algae contacting live corals, and by an in situ experiment demonstrating higher coral mortality in contact with algae left undisturbed than with algae from which all mobile epifauna were periodically removed. Among the main contributing mechanisms, we suggest that algal contact produces decaying coral tissue that attracts the corallivore and enhances its aggregation behavior. Our study demonstrates an indirect effect pathway by which algae can impact corals, which shares similarities with the classic models of apparent competition and habitat facilitation.

Discussion Seasonality in coral growth and branching Based on the results o f  this study, coral growth within one year is perceived to exhibit a certain pattern. High growth rates occur during the relatively cooler times of  the year, and low growth rates during the warmer periods. Cool months in the Philippines coincide roughly with the greatest intensity of  the northeast monsoon, which is approximately from November  to January. During the transition to the other monsoon regime in the country, the southwest, temperatures observed during the period of  the study were rather variable, but increased on the average. Temperatures then decreased gradually during the rainy months of  July through October towards the shift once more to the northeast monsoon. It is possible that the apparent seasonality in coral growth observed in Bolinao is a more general phenomenon,  particularly with respect to temperate species which are subject to larger tempera- ture fluctuations. Knowledge of  seasonality would have applications in management,  such as in coral transplanta- tion and harvesting schemes.

For dislodged corals almost all produced brooded larvae and there was, overall, a reduced output. Growth was decreased and there was a reduction in reproductive potential and no change in lipids. Gray (1989) suggested that the application of a stressor may cause an alarm reac- tion followed by compensation and a return to normal and that, if the application continues, the organism may die. He hypothesizes that initially an organism will divert energy from growth into reproduction but on further application of the stressor the fecundity will decrease. Thompson (1983, 1984) found that sea urchins on a depleted food ration decreased their gametic output but, when considered with their accompa- nying decrease in growth, this represented an increase in reproductive effort. As the mortality figures suggest, the dislodged corals were dying or at least not performing well. These results suggest that they may have shifted allocation away from growth to reproduction. Although the IRP was reduced in comparison with corals which were not dislodged, this may not reflect the reproductive effort of the corals as the proportion of total energy used for reproduction may have increased,

Once corallivores are attracted to the zone of interaction, mechanisms leading to coral mortality remain to be elucidated. Gut contents of H. carunculata have been found to include coral tissue (Marsden 1963), confirming that the worm can feed on corals. Aggregative feeding behavior of predators, in particu-lar scavengers, can cause high mortality in prey subject to even a small degree of stress and/or damage (Ramsay and Kaiser 1998) and constitutes an impor-tant mechanism driving trait-mediated indirect inter-actions (Werner and Peacor 2003). For example, Schmitt (1987) showed that adding bivalves to plots increased predation on gastropods due to aggregative behavior of invertebrate predators. In our study, the worms showed a marked aggregation behavior in H. opuntia, which appeared to be further enhanced by the presence of live coral. Halimeda alone is able to damage and weaken corals, as confirmed by our algal treat-ments without corallivores and laboratory work (Smith et al. 2006). The alga may thus lead to high coral mortality by enhancing the aggregative behavior of H. carunculata. The worms may also modify the physical, chemical and microbial microenvironment of over-grown corals, by excreting particulate wastes and leaving remains of decaying tissues that can then be colonized by microbes, increase oxygen demand, and reduce pH. These effects are likely to be exacerbated by the conditions of reduced flow underneath the algal canopy and to add on to the already detrimental effects of algae (Hauri et al. 2010). Moreover, a number of corallivores, including H. carunculata, have been implicated as potential disease vectors (Sussman et al. 2003, Williams and Miller 2005). Our field experiment supported a relationship between H. opuntia and white plague signs, reinforcing earlier work at the same site (Nugues et al. 2004). However, although trends were suggestive of a role of the algal-associated epifauna in the disease process, differences in disease prevalence between algal treatments with and without epifauna were not significant. Corallivores may also reduce coral disease progression through selective consumption of diseased coral tissues (Chong-Seng et al. 2011). Thus, their role in coral diseases is still equivocal.
